newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Seagate expects tight disk drive supply.
newsitem.headline: Seagate expects tight disk drive supply.

text.p: Seagate Technology Inc expects the supply of disk drives to remain tight in the second quarter of this year due to a shortage of recording heads, a senior company official said on Wednesday.
The world largest's independent disk drive maker also remains bullish on demand into its 1998 fiscal year, when it expects to spend US$1 billion on expanding production capacity.

Joel Stead, Seagate's vice president and managing director of Asia Pacific sales and marketing, told a news briefing the tight supply of disk drives would mean the company would continue to allocate products to customers on a rationed basis.
"In Q1 (calendar year 1997), we were on allocation for virtually all our products. It appears this situation could continue through Q2 calendar year," Stead said.
"In terms of severity, it's hard to say. Desktop products continue to be on heavy, heavy allocation in all capacities.

"We're ramping our production of drives but there continues to be a shortage of recording heads, both in films and MR (magneto-resistive heads). We are increasing our capacity for recording heads and we are also securing outside vendors to supply us heads," he said.
Stead was speaking at a briefing on the company's recently released third-quarter results.
Seagate produces about 80 percent of its recording heads internally.

In its third quarter ended March 1997, Seagate posted net profit of US$256.8 million on revenue of $2.5 billion. This compared with a net loss of $157.5 million on sales of $2.1 billion in the same period a year ago.
The third-quarter performance was better than the second quarter, when Seagate made a net profit of $212.6 million on revenue of $2.4 billion.
Third-quarter gross margins rose to 25.2 percent from 22.6 percent the previous quarter.
"We believe we need to stay in the 22 to 24 percent area in order to continue to invest in R&D (research and development) and...push products to the market out," Stead said.
Its margins had been lifted by less price erosion due to the tight supply and by benefits from its recent merger with fellow U.S. disk drive maker Conner Peripherals, he said.
Stead said the company was bullish on the industry and repeated its previous plan to spend US$1 billion in fiscal 1998 to boost capacity.

"Most of our investments are in Asia, so most of it will be in Asia. Disk drive consumption is supposed to grow another 20 percent. With us wanting to maintain share or gain share in some areas, that means we have to increase our capacity a minimum of 20 percent," he said.
For fiscal 1997, Seagate would end up spending about $800 million out of its originally targeted S$1 billion in capital expenditure, he said.
Seagate recently said it would spend $30 million to raise capacity in its printed circuit board assembly plant in Johor, Malaysia, by June 1998.
It is also investing $32 million to expand disk drive production in China and will spend another $300 million to boost disk drive recording head operations in the Philippines in 1997.

He said the company could move its production of disk drives for mobile computers out of its plant in Singapore, but a likely location had not yet been decided. More than 90 percent of the Singapore disk drive output was in high-end drives, he added.
